title: Unconditional Quantum Advantage For Sampling With Shallow Circuits
authors: Adam Bene Watts And Natalie Parham
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2188 (2026).

Recent work by Bravyi, Gosset, and Koenig showed that there exists a search problem that a constant-depth quantum circuit can solve, but that any constant-depth classical circuit with bounded fan-in cannot. They also pose the question: Can we achieve a similar proof of separation for an input-independent sampling task? In this paper, we show that the answer to this question is yes when the number of random input bits given to the classical circuit is bounded. We introduce a distribution [MATH] over [MATH] and construct a constant-depth uniform quantum circuit family [MATH] such that [MATH] samples from a distribution close to [MATH] in total variation distance. For any [MATH] we also prove, unconditionally, that any classical circuit with bounded fan-in gates that takes as input [MATH] i.i.d. Bernouli random variables with entropy [MATH] and produces output close to [MATH] in total variation distance has depth [MATH]. This gives an unconditional proof that constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from distributions that can't be reproduced by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits, even up to additive error. We also show a similar separation between constant-depth quantum circuits with advice and classical circuits with bounded fan-in and fan-out, but access to an unbounded number of i.i.d random inputs. The distribution [MATH] and classical circuit lower bounds are inspired by work of Viola, in which he shows a different (but related) distribution cannot be sampled from approximately by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits.

tldr: This paper proves an unconditional separation between constant-depth quantum circuits and constant-depth classical circuits for a sampling task, given bounded classical randomness.
motivation: The authors aim to extend the known separation for search problems to sampling tasks, which is a fundamental question in quantum complexity theory.
method: They introduce a specific distribution and construct a constant-depth quantum circuit that samples from it, then prove a lower bound on the depth of any classical circuit with bounded fan-in that approximates the same distribution, using techniques inspired by Viola.
result: They show that constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from a distribution that cannot be reproduced by constant-depth classical circuits with bounded fan-in, even with additive error, when the classical circuit has limited random bits.
conclusion: This provides an unconditional quantum advantage for sampling with shallow circuits, strengthening the case for quantum computational supremacy in a restricted setting.

title: Quantifiers And Witnesses For The Nonclassicality Of Measurements And Of States
authors: Yujie Zhang, Yìlè Yīng, And David Schmid
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2180 (2026).

In recent work [Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050], we proposed a unified notion of nonclassicality that applies to arbitrary processes in quantum theory, including individual quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof. This notion is derived from the principle of generalized noncontextuality, but in a novel manner that applies to individual processes rather than full experiments or theories. In the present work, we develop semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of states, sources, measurements, and sets thereof. These theory-dependent methods complement theory-independent approaches based on noncontextuality inequalities. We demonstrate the framework through a variety of explicit examples.

.
tldr: This paper develops semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof, based on generalized noncontextuality.
motivation: To provide practical tools for detecting nonclassicality in individual quantum processes, complementing theory-independent noncontextuality inequalities.
method: The authors formulate semidefinite programs that serve as certificates and witnesses for nonclassicality, applicable to states, sources, measurements, and sets, and demonstrate them with examples.
result: They present explicit SDP-based methods that can certify nonclassicality in various scenarios, as illustrated through examples.
conclusion: The proposed framework offers a versatile and computationally efficient approach to witness nonclassicality, advancing the operational characterization of quantum resources.

title: Stabilizer Ranks, Barnes Wall Lattices And Magic Monotones
authors: Amolak Ratan Kalra And Pulkit Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2179 (2026).

In 2024, Kliuchnikov and Schönnenbeck showed a connection between the Barnes Wall lattices, stabilizer states and Clifford operations. In this work, we study their results and relate them to the problem of lower bounding stabilizer ranks. We show the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which reproduces the linear-by-log lower bound for [MATH], i.e, on the approximate stabilizer rank of [MATH]. In fact, we show that the lower bound holds even when the fidelity between the approximation and [MATH] is exponentially small, which is currently the best lower bound in this regime. Next, we define a new magic monotone for pure states, the Barnes Wall norm, and its corresponding approximate variant. We upper bound these monotones by the [MATH]-count of state preparation, and also by the stabilizer ranks. In particular, the upper bound given by the [MATH]-count is tight, in the sense that we exhibit states that achieve the bound. Apart from these results, we give a Fidelity Amplification algorithm, which provides a trade-off between approximation error and the stabilizer rank. As a corollary, it gives us a way to compose approximate stabilizer decompositions into approximate decompositions of their tensor products. Finally, we provide an alternate, elementary proof of the existence and density of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks, which was first proven by Lovitz and Steffan (2022), where they used results from algebraic geometry.

.
tldr: This paper connects Barnes Wall lattices to stabilizer ranks, providing new lower bounds and a magic monotone.
motivation: To better understand and bound the stabilizer rank, a key resource in quantum computation, and to introduce new magic monotones.
method: The authors study the connection between Barnes Wall lattices and stabilizer states, derive quantitative lower bounds on stabilizer fidelity, define a new magic monotone (Barnes Wall norm), and provide a fidelity amplification algorithm.
result: They obtain the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which is best in the exponentially small fidelity regime, and show tight upper bounds for the new monotone via T-count.
conclusion: The work advances the theory of stabilizer ranks and magic monotones, offering new tools for quantum resource theories.

title: A Complete Theory Of The Clifford Commutant
authors: Lennart Bittel, Jens Eisert, Lorenzo Leone, Antonio A. Mele, And Salvatore F.E. Oliviero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2171 (2026).

The Clifford group plays a central role in quantum information science. It is the building block for many error-correcting schemes and matches the first three moments of the Haar measure over the unitary group-a property that is essential for a broad range of quantum algorithms, with applications in pseudorandomness, learning theory, benchmarking, and entanglement distillation. At the heart of understanding many properties of the Clifford group lies the Clifford commutant: the set of operators that commute with [MATH]-fold tensor powers of Clifford unitaries. Previous understanding of this commutant has been limited to relatively small values of [MATH], constrained by the number of qubits [MATH]. In this work, we develop a complete theory of the Clifford commutant. Our first result provides an explicit orthogonal basis for the commutant and computes its dimension for arbitrary [MATH] and [MATH]. We also introduce an alternative and easy-to-manipulate basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators. We show that this basis is generated by products of permutations, which generate the unitary group commutant, and at most three other operators. Additionally, we develop a graphical calculus allowing a diagrammatic manipulation of elements of this basis. These results enable a wealth of applications: among others, we characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, whose success probability also offers an operational interpretation to stabilizer entropies. Finally, we show that these results also generalize to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

.
tldr: This paper provides a complete theory of the Clifford commutant, offering explicit bases and a graphical calculus, with applications to magic measures and stabilizer property testing.
motivation: The Clifford group is central to quantum information, but the structure of its commutant was only partially understood for small tensor powers and qubit numbers. A complete characterization is needed for various applications.
method: The authors develop an explicit orthogonal basis for the Clifford commutant for arbitrary tensor power and qubit number, introduce an alternative basis of isotropic sums of Pauli operators, and provide a graphical calculus for manipulation.
result: They compute the dimension of the commutant, show the basis is generated by permutations and at most three other operators, and apply the results to characterize measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing.
conclusion: The complete theory of the Clifford commutant enables a wealth of applications in quantum information, including magic quantification and property testing, and extends to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

title: Measurement Incompatibility In Bayesian Multiparameter Quantum Estimation
authors: Francesco Albarelli, Dominic Branford, And Jesús Rubio
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2192 (2026).

We present a comprehensive and pedagogical formulation of Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation. Within this framework, we analyse the role of measurement incompatibility and establish its quantitative effect on attainable precision. We achieve this by deriving upper bounds based on the pretty good measurement – a notion from hypothesis testing – combined with the evaluation of the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound. In general, we prove that, as in the many-copy regime of local estimation theory, incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss relative to the idealised scenario in which individually optimal measurements are assumed jointly implementable. Therefore, in practical situations, the latter may provide a sufficient and computationally efficient benchmark without solving the full optimisation problem. Our results, which we illustrate through applications of discrete phase imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing, provide analytical and numerical tools for assessing ultimate precision limits and the role of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology, including an open-source package for all the bounds discussed here.

.
tldr: This paper provides a comprehensive Bayesian framework for multiparameter quantum estimation, deriving bounds on measurement incompatibility and showing that it can at most double the minimum loss compared to the ideal joint measurement scenario.
motivation: Multiparameter quantum estimation is crucial for quantum metrology, but measurement incompatibility limits achievable precision. The authors aim to quantify this effect in the Bayesian regime, which is more practical for finite resources.
method: They formulate Bayesian multiparameter estimation and derive upper bounds using the pretty good measurement and the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound. They also provide an open-source package for computing these bounds.
result: They prove that measurement incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss relative to the ideal scenario, and illustrate this with examples like discrete phase imaging and qubit sensing.
conclusion: The results provide practical benchmarks for Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology, showing that the ideal joint measurement assumption is often sufficient, and offer tools for assessing ultimate precision limits.

title: Modulator-Assisted Zeno Control Of Energy Transfer In Quantum Batteries
authors: Songbo Xie, Manas Sajjan, Ashok Ajoy, And Sabre Kais
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2178 (2026).

Efficient operation of quantum batteries requires not only fast energy transfer but also the ability to halt the charging process to prevent reverse flow. Existing approaches typically rely on direct control of the charger-battery interaction, which can be experimentally demanding. Here we propose a modulator-assisted quantum battery protocol that enables indirect control of energy transfer while keeping the interaction always on. By applying repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit, we exploit a Zeno-like mechanism to dynamically reshape the effective Hamiltonian and switch the charger-battery coupling on and off. We demonstrate this mechanism in a minimal three-body model and show that it remains effective beyond the ideal fast-control limit. We further extend the protocol to a collective many-body architecture, where it preserves the characteristic enhancement of charging power, scaling as [MATH] with the number of battery units. We also discuss a possible implementation in an NV-[MATH]C spin platform. Our results establish modulator-assisted Zeno control as a scalable route to regulating energy transfer in quantum batteries.

.
tldr: This paper proposes a modulator-assisted Zeno control protocol for quantum batteries, enabling indirect on/off switching of energy transfer while keeping the interaction always on.
motivation: Efficient quantum battery operation requires halting charging to prevent reverse flow, but direct control of the charger-battery interaction is experimentally demanding. The authors aim to achieve indirect control using a modulator qubit.
method: They apply repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit, exploiting a Zeno-like mechanism to dynamically reshape the effective Hamiltonian and switch the charger-battery coupling on and off. They demonstrate this in a minimal three-body model and extend to a collective many-body architecture.
result: The protocol works beyond the ideal fast-control limit, preserves the collective charging power enhancement scaling with the number of battery units, and is feasible in an NV-13C spin platform.
conclusion: Modulator-assisted Zeno control offers a scalable route to regulating energy transfer in quantum batteries, addressing a key challenge in quantum thermodynamics.

title: Non-commutative Optimization Problems With Differential Constraints
authors: Mateus Araújo, Andrew J. P. Garner, And Miguel Navascues
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2169 (2026).

Non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) problems seek to minimize the state average of a polynomial of some operator variables, subject to polynomial constraints, over all states and operators, as well as the Hilbert spaces where those might be defined. Many of these problems are known to admit a complete hierarchy of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. In this work, we consider a variant of NPO problems where a subset of the operator variables satisfies a system of ordinary differential equations. We prove that, under mild conditions of operator boundedness, for every such problem one can construct a standard NPO problem with the same solution. This allows us to define a complete hierarchy of SDPs to tackle the original differential problem. We apply this method to bound averages of local observables in quantum spin systems subject to a Hamiltonian evolution (i.e., a quench). We find that, even in the thermodynamic limit of infinitely many sites, low levels of the hierarchy provide very good approximations for reasonably long evolution times.

.
tldr: This paper extends non-commutative polynomial optimization to handle differential constraints, providing a complete SDP hierarchy and applying it to bound observables in quantum spin systems after a quench.
motivation: Many quantum information problems involve dynamics, but standard NPO cannot directly handle differential constraints. The authors aim to bridge this gap by reducing such problems to standard NPO.
method: They prove that under boundedness conditions, any NPO with differential constraints can be transformed into an equivalent standard NPO, enabling the use of existing SDP hierarchies. They then apply this to quench dynamics in spin systems.
result: The method yields tight bounds on local observables even in the thermodynamic limit, with low hierarchy levels providing good approximations for reasonably long evolution times.
conclusion: This work provides a new tool for analyzing quantum dynamics with optimization techniques, potentially useful for quantum information and many-body physics.

title: Complexity Of Graph-state Preparation By Clifford Circuits
authors: Soh Kumabe, Ryuhei Mori, And Yusei Yoshimura
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2165 (2026).

In this work, we study the complexity of graph-state preparation in a general model of quantum algorithms that allows measurements in the computational basis, single-qubit Clifford operations, and two-qubit Clifford operations. We define the CZ-complexity of a graph state [MATH] as the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations required to generate [MATH] from [MATH] for some [MATH]. Equivalently, every optimal algorithm can be taken to use only controlled-Z (CZ) gates as its two-qubit Clifford operations. We then give a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations. Specifically, [MATH] can be generated from another graph state [MATH] by an algorithm of CZ-complexity at most [MATH] if and only if [MATH] can be obtained from [MATH] by vertex deletions, local complementations and at most [MATH] elementary edge-complementations. Here, an elementary edge-complementation toggles either a single edge, all edges between one vertex and the neighborhood of another, or all edges between the neighborhoods of two non-adjacent vertices. Using this characterization, we relate CZ-complexity to rank-width. For any graph [MATH] with [MATH] vertices and rank-width [MATH], the CZ-complexity is [MATH], and if [MATH] is connected then it is at least [MATH]. We also show that these bounds are close to optimal. Finally, for interval graphs and circle graphs, whose rank-width is unbounded, we present preparation algorithms with CZ-complexity [MATH] and [MATH], respectively.

tldr: This paper characterizes the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations (CZ-complexity) needed to prepare graph states, linking it to graph transformations and rank-width.
motivation: Understanding the resource cost of preparing graph states is crucial for quantum information processing, as graph states are key resources for measurement-based quantum computing and quantum error correction.
method: The authors define CZ-complexity and prove a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations using vertex deletions, local complementations, and edge-complementations. They then relate CZ-complexity to rank-width and provide algorithms for interval and circle graphs.

conclusion: The work provides a rigorous complexity-theoretic framework for graph-state preparation, offering both theoretical bounds and practical algorithms, which is valuable for optimizing quantum circuits.

title: Catalytic $z$-rotations In Constant $T$-depth
authors: Isaac H. Kim
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2191 (2026).

We show that the [MATH]-depth of any single-qubit [MATH]-rotation can be reduced to [MATH] if a certain catalyst state is available. To achieve an [MATH]-approximation, it suffices to have a catalyst state of size polynomial in [MATH]. This implies that [MATH] admits a finite universal gate set consisting of Clifford+[MATH]. In particular, there are catalytic constant [MATH]-depth circuits that approximate multi-qubit Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform arbitrarily well. We also show that the catalyst state can be prepared in time polynomial in [MATH].

.
tldr: This paper shows that any single-qubit z-rotation can be approximated to arbitrary precision with constant T-depth using a catalyst state of polynomial size, implying a finite universal gate set for quantum computation.
motivation: Reducing T-depth is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation, as T gates are expensive. The paper aims to achieve constant T-depth for arbitrary rotations, which is a significant improvement over existing methods.
method: The authors construct a catalyst state that enables the implementation of z-rotations with constant T-depth, and they prove that the catalyst state can be prepared efficiently in polynomial time.
result: They demonstrate that any single-qubit z-rotation can be approximated with constant T-depth, and that multi-qubit gates like Toffoli, adder, and QFT can also be approximated with constant T-depth using this catalyst.
conclusion: The existence of a finite universal gate set with constant T-depth for arbitrary rotations is established, which has implications for reducing the overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Shadow Pauli Flow: Characterising Determinism In MBQCs Involving Pauli Measurements
authors: Mehdi Mhalla, Simon Perdrix, And Luc Sanselme
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2163 (2026).

We introduce a new characterisation of determinism in Measurement-Based Quantum Computing (MBQC). The one-way model consists in performing local measurements over a large entangled state represented by a graph. The ability to perform an overall deterministic computation requires a correction strategy because of the non-determinism of each measurement. The existence of such a correction strategy depends on the underlying open graph, which is a description of the resource state together with the basis of the performed measurements. GFlow is a well-known graphical characterisation of robust determinism in MBQC when every measurement is performed in some specific planes of the Bloch sphere. While Pauli measurements are ubiquitous in MBQC, GFlow fails to be necessary for determinism when a measurement-based quantum computation involves Pauli measurements. Pauli Flow was designed as a generalisation of GFlow to handle MBQC with Pauli measurements, and guarantees robust determinism, however, it has been shown more recently that it fails to be a necessary condition. Our contribution is twofold. First, we demonstrate that Pauli flow is actually necessary for robust determinism in a weaker sense: given an open graph, i.e. a resource state, a deterministic computation can be driven iff it has a Pauli flow. However, the Pauli flows do not reflect all the possible correction strategies over a particular resource state, and properties like measurement order or computational depth are not necessarily reflected by a Pauli flow. Thus, to characterise determinism in full generality, we introduce a further extension called Shadow Pauli Flow that we prove necessary and sufficient for robust determinism: An MBQC is robustly deterministic if and only if its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow. Furthermore, we show that Shadow Pauli flow can be computed in polynomial time.

.
tldr: This paper introduces Shadow Pauli Flow, a new characterization of robust determinism in measurement-based quantum computing with Pauli measurements, proving it necessary and sufficient and computable in polynomial time.
motivation: Previous characterizations like GFlow and Pauli Flow are either insufficient or not necessary for determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, limiting the understanding of correction strategies.
method: The authors define Shadow Pauli Flow as an extension of Pauli Flow, and prove that an MBQC is robustly deterministic if and only if its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow, also providing a polynomial-time algorithm.
result: They demonstrate that Pauli flow is necessary for robust determinism in a weaker sense, but Shadow Pauli Flow fully characterizes determinism, capturing all correction strategies and measurement orders.
conclusion: Shadow Pauli Flow provides a complete and efficient characterization of determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, advancing the theory of measurement-based quantum computing.

title: Quantum Nonlocality Without Entanglement And State Discrimination Measures
authors: Shayeef Murshid, Tathagata Gupta, Vincent Russo, And Somshubhro Bandyopadhyay
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2174 (2026).

An ensemble of product states is said to exhibit “quantum nonlocality without entanglement” if it cannot be optimally discriminated using local operations and classical communication (LOCC). We show that this property can depend on the chosen discrimination measure. Specifically, we construct a family of ensembles, each consisting of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states, for which LOCC fails to achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but succeeds in achieving optimal unambiguous discrimination. We further extend our construction to multipartite systems and provide strong numerical evidence that a similar separation between local and global optima is present for minimum-error discrimination, but not for unambiguous discrimination.

.
tldr: This paper shows that quantum nonlocality without entanglement can depend on the discrimination measure, constructing ensembles where LOCC fails for minimum-error but succeeds for unambiguous discrimination.
motivation: To understand whether the property of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is robust to the choice of discrimination measure, which is fundamental for quantum state discrimination and its applications.
method: The authors construct explicit ensembles of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states and analyze their optimal discrimination under LOCC for both minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination, extending to multipartite systems with numerical evidence.
result: They find a separation: LOCC cannot achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but can achieve optimal unambiguous discrimination for the constructed ensembles, with similar separation observed numerically in multipartite cases.
conclusion: The property of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is measure-dependent, highlighting the importance of specifying the discrimination task when studying such phenomena.

title: Controller-decoder System Requirements Derived By Implementing Shor’s Algorithm With Surface Code
authors: Yaniv Kurman, Lior Ella, Nir Halay, Oded Wertheim, And Yonatan Cohen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2170 (2026).

Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is regarded as the most promising path to quantum advantage. The success of QEC relies on achieving quantum gate fidelities below the error threshold of the QEC code, while accurately decoding errors through classical processing of the QEC stabilizer measurements. In this paper, we uncover the critical system-level requirements from a controller-decoder system (CDS) necessary to successfully execute the next milestone in QEC: a non-Clifford circuit. Using a representative non-Clifford circuit, of Shor factorization algorithm for the number 21, we convert the logical-level circuit to a QEC surface code circuit and finally to the physical level circuit. By taking into account realistic implementation aspects using typical superconducting qubit processor parameters, we reveal a broad range of core requirements from any CDS aimed at performing error corrected quantum computation. Our findings indicate that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must remain within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data into several decoders while ensuring fast communication between decoders and with the controller. By extending existing simulation techniques, we simulate the complete fault-tolerant factorization circuit at the physical level, demonstrating that near-term hardware performance in the scale of 0.1% physical error rates and 1000 qubits, are sufficient for a successful circuit execution. Overall, the requirements outlined here set the stage for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

.
tldr: This paper derives system-level requirements for a controller-decoder system to execute non-Clifford quantum error correction circuits, using Shor's algorithm for factoring 21 as a representative example.
motivation: The next milestone in quantum error correction is executing non-Clifford circuits, which requires meeting stringent system-level requirements for the controller-decoder system. The paper aims to uncover these requirements to guide near-term experimental realizations.
method: The authors convert a logical-level Shor's algorithm circuit for factoring 21 into a surface code circuit and then to a physical-level circuit, incorporating realistic superconducting qubit parameters. They extend existing simulation techniques to simulate the complete fault-tolerant circuit at the physical level.
result: They find that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must be within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data among multiple decoders with fast communication. They demonstrate that near-term hardware with ~0.1% physical error rates and ~1000 qubits is sufficient for successful execution.
conclusion: The requirements outlined set the stage for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits, providing a practical roadmap for advancing quantum error correction.

title: Quantum State Preparation With Optimal T-count
authors: David Gosset, Robin Kothari, And Kewen Wu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2168 (2026).

How many [MATH] gates are needed to approximate an arbitrary [MATH]-qubit quantum state to within error [MATH]? Improving prior work of Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer, we show that the optimal asymptotic scaling is [MATH] if we allow ancilla qubits. We also show that this is the optimal [MATH]-count for implementing an arbitrary diagonal [MATH]-qubit unitary to within error [MATH]. We describe applications in which a tensor product of many single-qubit unitaries can be synthesized in parallel for the price of one.

.
tldr: This paper determines the optimal T-count for approximating arbitrary quantum states and diagonal unitaries, showing that ancilla qubits enable a scaling of O(4^n n) and that tensor products of single-qubit unitaries can be synthesized in parallel for the price of one.
motivation: The number of T gates is a critical resource for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and prior work left a gap between lower and upper bounds. This work aims to close that gap and provide tight asymptotic bounds.
method: The authors improve upon prior work by Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer, using techniques from quantum circuit synthesis and approximation theory to construct circuits with optimal T-count, and prove matching lower bounds.
result: They show that the optimal asymptotic scaling for approximating an arbitrary n-qubit state to error epsilon is O(4^n n) when ancilla qubits are allowed, and similarly for diagonal unitaries. They also demonstrate parallel synthesis of many single-qubit unitaries at the cost of one.
conclusion: The results settle the optimal T-count for state preparation and diagonal unitary synthesis, providing practical guidance for resource estimation in fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Robust Topological Quantum State Transfer With Long-range Interactions In Rydberg Arrays
authors: Siri Raupach, Beatriz Olmos, And Mathias B. M. Svendsen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2190 (2026).

We develop a theoretical framework for fast, robust and high-fidelity topological quantum state transfer in one-dimensional systems with long-range couplings, motivated by chains of Rydberg atoms with dipole–dipole interactions. Such long-range interactions naturally give rise to extended Su–Schrieffer–Heeger and Rice–Mele models supporting topologically protected edge states. We show that these edge states enable high-fidelity edge-to-edge excitation transfer using both time-independent protocols, based on coherent edge state dynamics, and time-dependent protocols, based on adiabatic modulation of system parameters. Long-range couplings play a central role by enhancing the relevant energy gaps, leading to a substantial improvement in transfer efficiency compared to nearest neighbour models. The resulting transfer is robust against positional disorder, reflecting its topological origin and highlighting the potential of long-range interacting platforms for reliable quantum state transfer.

.
tldr: This paper presents a theoretical framework for robust topological quantum state transfer in long-range interacting Rydberg arrays, leveraging edge states to achieve high-fidelity transfer.
motivation: Quantum state transfer is crucial for quantum networks, and topological protection can enhance robustness. Long-range interactions in Rydberg arrays may improve transfer efficiency compared to nearest-neighbor models.
method: The authors develop theoretical models based on extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger and Rice-Mele chains with long-range couplings, analyzing both time-independent and time-dependent (adiabatic) protocols for edge-to-edge excitation transfer.
result: Long-range couplings enhance energy gaps, leading to substantially improved transfer efficiency and robustness against positional disorder, outperforming nearest-neighbor models.
conclusion: Long-range interacting platforms like Rydberg arrays show promise for reliable quantum state transfer, with topological protection offering robustness.

title: Efficient Graph State Generation In Linear Optics
authors: Seungbeom Chin And William John Munro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2189 (2026).

Graph states are central resources for quantum information processing, supporting applications in computation, communication, and error correction. In photonic systems, they are typically assembled from smaller entangled states using probabilistic fusion gates, which demand many photons and suffer from low success rates. We present an optimized scheme for directly generating caterpillar graph states (CGSs)—essential resource states for constructing high-dimensional lattice graph states—using only single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements. Based on the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture, our method produces CGSs efficiently. For CGSs of length [MATH], it requires [MATH] fewer photons and achieves a success rate [MATH] times higher than fusion-based approaches. These results demonstrate that the LQG picture provides a powerful and flexible route to generating complex photonic graph states for efficient quantum information processing.

.
tldr: This paper presents an optimized scheme for generating caterpillar graph states using linear optics, achieving higher efficiency than fusion-based methods.
motivation: Graph states are essential for quantum information processing, but photonic generation via fusion gates is inefficient. The authors aim to improve the generation of caterpillar graph states, which are building blocks for larger lattice states.
method: The method uses the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture, employing single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements to directly generate caterpillar graph states without fusion gates.
result: The scheme requires fewer photons and achieves a success rate several times higher than fusion-based approaches for caterpillar graph states of length n.
conclusion: The LQG picture provides a powerful and flexible route to generating complex photonic graph states, potentially advancing photonic quantum information processing.

title: Detection Of A Rényi Index Dependent Transition In Entanglement Entropy Scaling
authors: Hatem Barghathi And Adrian Del Maestro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2184 (2026).

The scaling of entanglement with subsystem size encodes key information about phases and criticality, but the von Neumann entropy is costly to access in experiments and simulations, often requiring full state tomography. The second Rényi entropy is readily measured using two-copy protocols and is often used as a proxy for the von Neumann entanglement entropy, where it is assumed to track its asymptotic scaling. Sugino and Korepiny (Int. J. Mod. Phys. B 32, 1850306 (2018)) revealed that in the ground state of some highly constrained spin models, the scaling of the von Neumann and Rényi entropies can differ, varying from power law to logarithmic scaling as a function of the Rényi index. Here, we construct a number-conserving many-body state that demonstrates a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling, generalizing previous results to the case of interacting fermions. We introduce a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy built from charge-resolved Rényi entropies that can provide a protocol for diagnosing anomalous entanglement scaling from experimentally accessible data.

.
tldr: This paper constructs a number-conserving fermionic state exhibiting a Rényi-index-dependent transition in entanglement entropy scaling, and introduces a symmetry-aware lower bound on von Neumann entropy from charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
motivation: The von Neumann entropy is hard to measure, so Rényi entropies are often used as proxies. However, in some constrained models, their scaling can differ, and this work aims to generalize such behavior to interacting fermions and provide an experimentally accessible diagnostic.
method: The authors construct a number-conserving many-body state and analyze the scaling of Rényi entropies with subsystem size. They also derive a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy using charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
result: They demonstrate a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling, generalizing previous results to interacting fermions, and propose a protocol for diagnosing anomalous scaling from experimental data.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework and experimental protocol for detecting Rényi-index-dependent entanglement scaling, which is relevant for quantum information and many-body physics.

title: Entanglement-assisted Quasi-cyclic Quantum Low-density Parity-check Codes Over Qubits
authors: Pavan Kumar, Abhi Kumar Sharma, Karthik Bharadwaj, And Shayan Srinivasa Garani
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2181 (2026).

We construct several families of entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC (EA-QC-QLDPC) codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices. The entanglement-unassisted portion of the joint Tanner graph of the proposed EA-QC-QLDPC code derived from two distinct classical QC-LDPC codes is free of 4-cycles. Notably, one of the proposed families constructed from two distinct classical codes requires only a [MATH] shared Bell pair between the quantum transmitter and receiver, highlighting its resource efficiency. We also analytically determine the exact code rates for some of the proposed constructions. Furthermore, two of the proposed families of EA-QC-QLDPC codes are derived from a single classical code whose Tanner graphs possess girth greater than six, further enhancing their error-correcting performance. We also propose an encoding scheme with improved complexity by exploiting the proposed code structure. The performance of the proposed codes is assessed under both random and burst error models under the depolarizing and Markovian noise actions. Simulation results reveal nearly one order of improvement in error-correction performance with the quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum (QBLNMS) decoder compared to the layered binary sum-product decoder over both depolarizing and Markovian channels. Using the QBLNMS decoder over a quaternary alphabet, we demonstrate that correlated Pauli errors can be effectively handled within the decoding framework. Furthermore, under the QBLNMS decoding, the proposed codes achieve [MATH] performance improvements compared to prior works and can effectively handle both random and burst errors. The code constructions are scalable across various coding rates and quantum payloads, crucial for practical quantum communication and computing systems.

.
tldr: This paper constructs entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC codes with improved error-correction performance and resource efficiency.
motivation: Quantum error correction is essential for reliable quantum communication and computation, and constructing efficient quantum LDPC codes with good performance is a key challenge.
method: The authors construct EA-QC-QLDPC codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices, ensuring 4-cycle-free Tanner graphs and deriving exact code rates. They also propose an encoding scheme and evaluate decoding with QBLNMS and layered binary sum-product decoders.
result: The proposed codes show nearly an order of magnitude improvement in error-correction performance with QBLNMS decoder, and one family requires only one shared Bell pair, demonstrating resource efficiency.
conclusion: The scalable constructions and improved decoding performance make these codes promising for practical quantum communication and computing systems.

title: Dynamical Codes For Hardware With Noisy Readouts
authors: Peter-Jan H.S. Derks, Alex Townsend-Teague, Jens Eisert, Markus S. Kesselring, Oscar Higgott, And Benjamin J. Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2176 (2026).

Dynamical stabilizer codes may offer a practical route to large-scale quantum computation. Such codes are defined by a schedule of error-detecting measurements, which allows for flexibility in their construction. In this work, we ask how best to optimise the measurement schedule of dynamically condensed colour codes in various limits of noise bias. We take a particular focus on the setting where measurements introduce more noise than unitary and idling operations – a noise model relevant to some hardware proposals. For measurement-biased noise models, we improve code performance by strategically repeating measurements within the schedule. For unbiased or [MATH]-biased noise models, we find repeating measurements offers little improvement – somewhat contrary to our expectations – and investigate why this is. To perform this analysis, we generalise a metric called the teraquop footprint to the teraquop volume. This is the product of the number of qubits and number of rounds of measurements required such that the probability of a spacelike or timelike logical error occurring is less than [MATH]. In most cases, we find differences in performance are primarily due to the number of rounds of measurements required, rather than the number of qubits – emphasising the importance of using the teraquop volume in the analysis. Additionally, our results provide another example of the importance of making use of correlated errors when decoding, in that using belief matching rather than minimum-weight perfect matching can turn a worst-performing code under a given noise model into a best-performing code.

.
tldr: This paper optimizes measurement schedules for dynamical color codes under biased noise, introducing the teraquop volume metric and showing that repeating measurements helps in measurement-biased regimes.
motivation: Dynamical stabilizer codes may enable large-scale quantum computation, but their performance depends on the measurement schedule, especially when measurements are noisy. The authors aim to optimize schedules for hardware with noisy readouts.
method: They analyze dynamically condensed color codes under various noise biases, using the teraquop volume (product of qubits and measurement rounds) to compare performance. They also compare decoding strategies: minimum-weight perfect matching vs. belief matching with correlated errors.
result: Repeating measurements improves performance under measurement-biased noise, but offers little benefit for unbiased or X-biased noise. The teraquop volume reveals that differences are mainly due to measurement rounds, not qubit count. Belief matching can turn a worst-performing code into a best-performing one.
conclusion: The teraquop volume is a valuable metric for assessing code performance, and optimizing measurement schedules and decoders is crucial for practical quantum error correction with noisy measurements.

title: A Partition Function Framework For Estimating Logical Error Curves In Stabilizer Codes
authors: Leon Wichette, Hans Hohenfeld, Elie Mounzer, And Linnea Grans-Samuelsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2175 (2026).

Based on the mapping between stabilizer quantum error correcting codes and disordered statistical mechanics models, we define a ratio of partition functions that measures the success probability for maximum partition function decoding, which at the Nishimori temperature corresponds to maximum likelihood (ML) decoding. We show that this ratio differs from the similarly defined order probability and describe the decoding strategy whose success rate is described by the order probability. We refer to the latter as a probabilistic partition function decoding and show that it is the strategy that at zero temperature corresponds to maximum probability (MP) decoding. Based on the difference between the two decoders, we discuss the possibility of a maximum partition function decodability boundary outside the order-disorder phase boundary. At zero temperature, the difference between the two ratios measures to what degree MP decoding can be improved by accounting for degeneracy among maximum probability errors, through methods such as ensembling. We consider in detail the example of the toric code under bitflip noise, which maps to the Random Bond Ising Model. We demonstrate that estimation of logical performance through decoding probability and order probability is more sample efficient than estimation by counting failures of the corresponding decoders, especially in the regime of low noise. We consider both uniform noise and noise where qubits are given individual error rates. The latter noise model lifts the degeneracy among maximum probability errors, but we show that ensembling remains useful as long as it also samples less probable errors. We also consider, in less detail, the color code under bitflip and depolarizing noise.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a partition function framework to estimate logical error rates in stabilizer codes, linking decoding success to statistical mechanics and demonstrating improved sample efficiency.
motivation: Accurate estimation of logical error rates is crucial for assessing quantum error correction performance, but existing methods can be sample-inefficient, especially at low noise.
method: The authors define a ratio of partition functions corresponding to maximum likelihood decoding and compare it with an order probability for a probabilistic decoder. They analyze the toric code under bitflip noise via the Random Bond Ising Model and also consider the color code.
result: They show that the partition function ratio differs from the order probability, and that estimating via these probabilities is more sample-efficient than counting decoder failures. They also discuss degeneracy effects and ensembling.
conclusion: The framework provides a new tool for analyzing decoding performance and suggests potential boundaries for decodability beyond phase transitions, with implications for improving decoding strategies.

title: Optimal Schedule Of Multi-channel Quantum Zeno Dragging With Application To Solving The k-SAT Problem
authors: Yipei Zhang, Alain Sarlette, Philippe Lewalle, Tathagata Karmakar, Thilo Scharnhorst, And K. Birgitta Whaley
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2167 (2026).

Quantum Zeno dragging enables the preparation of common eigenstates of a set of observables by frequent measurement and adiabatic-like modulation of the measurement basis. In this work, we present a deeper analysis of multi-channel Zeno dragging using generalized measurements, i.e. simultaneously measuring a set of non-commuting observables that vary slowly in time, to drag the state towards a target subspace. For concreteness, we will focus on a measurement-driven approach to solving k-SAT problems as examples. We first compute some analytical upper bounds on the convergence time, including the effect of finite measurement time resolution. We then apply optimal control theory to obtain the optimal dragging schedule that lower bounds the convergence time, for low-dimensional settings. This study provides a theoretical foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and its optimization, and also serves as a guide for designing optimal dragging schedules for quantum information tasks including measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes multi-channel quantum Zeno dragging with generalized measurements and applies optimal control to find schedules that minimize convergence time, with applications to solving k-SAT problems.
motivation: Quantum Zeno dragging can prepare target states via frequent measurements, but multi-channel versions with non-commuting observables lack rigorous analysis and optimization. The authors aim to provide theoretical foundations and optimal schedules for such protocols.
method: The authors derive analytical upper bounds on convergence time, including finite measurement resolution effects, and use optimal control theory to find schedules that lower-bound convergence time in low-dimensional settings.
result: They obtain analytical bounds and optimal dragging schedules that improve convergence time, demonstrated on k-SAT examples.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and offers guidance for designing optimal schedules for measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

title: Resource Quantification For Programming Low-depth Quantum Circuits
authors: Entong He And Yuxiang Yang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2166 (2026).

Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices pave the way for implementing quantum algorithms that offer quantum advantages over their classical counterparts. Due to the intrinsic noise and decoherence in the physical system, NISQ machines are naturally modeled as large-scale, low-depth quantum circuits. In practice, executing such circuits requires sending program states that encode the relevant instructions to a programmable quantum computer, typically through a cloud service. Existing programming approaches designed for generic unitary transformations are computationally inefficient in the low-depth setting, and therefore remain unsatisfactory. As such, to realize NISQ algorithms, it is crucial to find an efficient way to program low-depth circuits as the number of qubits [MATH] increases. Here, we investigate the circuit complexity and the size of quantum memory, known as the program cost, required to program low-depth brickwork circuits. We establish a tight worst-case program cost of [MATH] for universally programming low-depth brickwork circuits in the large-[MATH] regime. Moreover, we analyze the trade-off between the cost of describing the layout of local gates and the cost of programming them to implement the target unitaries via the light-cone argument. Our findings suggest that faithful gate-wise programming is essentially optimal in the low-depth regime.

.
tldr: This paper establishes tight bounds on the program cost (quantum memory size) required to universally program low-depth brickwork circuits, showing that gate-wise programming is essentially optimal in the low-depth regime.
motivation: Efficiently programming NISQ devices is crucial for realizing quantum advantages, but existing methods for generic unitary transformations are inefficient for low-depth circuits. The authors aim to find the minimal program cost for programming low-depth brickwork circuits.
method: The authors analyze the circuit complexity and quantum memory size needed to program low-depth brickwork circuits, using the light-cone argument to study the trade-off between describing local gate layouts and programming them.
result: They establish a tight worst-case program cost for universally programming low-depth brickwork circuits in the large-qubit regime, and show that faithful gate-wise programming is essentially optimal.
conclusion: The findings provide fundamental limits on the resources needed for programming low-depth quantum circuits, which is important for the practical implementation of NISQ algorithms.

title: Criticality-enhanced Quantum Sensing To A Dissipative Reservoir
authors: Xian-Kun Xin, Ze-Zhou Zhang, Qing-Shou Tan And Wei Wu
abstract: Criticality is widely regarded as a potential resource to boost the performance of quantum sensing. In existing protocols of criticality-enhanced quantum sensing, the criticality typically originates either from the probe or from the detected system itself. We here propose a scheme for sensing a dissipative reservoir based on the thermal criticality induced by the probe-reservoir interaction at finite temperature. It is revealed that the strong-coupling characteristics of the probe are able to create an additional thermal criticality, which significantly enhances the sensing performance. Our proposed scheme does not require precise dynamical control and is universal to different initial states, as it is built upon the equilibrium state generated by the natural dissipative dynamics of the probe. Expanding the scope of critical metrology, our findings pave a possible route toward high-precision quantum sensing.
tldr: This paper proposes a criticality-enhanced quantum sensing scheme for dissipative reservoirs, leveraging thermal criticality induced by probe-reservoir interactions at finite temperature.
motivation: Criticality is a known resource for quantum sensing, but existing protocols rely on criticality from the probe or system itself. This work aims to exploit criticality arising from the probe-reservoir interaction to sense reservoir properties without precise control.
method: The authors analyze a probe strongly coupled to a dissipative reservoir at finite temperature, showing that the strong coupling creates an additional thermal criticality. They use equilibrium states generated by natural dissipative dynamics and evaluate sensing performance near the critical point.
result: The thermal criticality significantly enhances sensing precision, and the scheme is universal to initial states and requires no precise dynamical control.
conclusion: The findings expand the scope of critical metrology and provide a route to high-precision quantum sensing of dissipative environments.

title: Quantum Resource Comparison For Two Leading Surface Code Lattice Surgery Approaches
authors: Tyler Leblond And Ryan S. Bennink
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2187 (2026).

Hamiltonian simulation is one of the most promising candidates for the demonstration of quantum advantage within the next ten years, and several studies have proposed end-to-end resource estimates for executing such algorithms on fault-tolerant quantum processors. Usually, these resource estimates are based upon the assumption that quantum error correction is implemented using the surface code, and that the best surface code compilation scheme involves serializing input circuits by eliminating all Clifford gates. This transformation is thought to make best use of the native multi-body measurement (lattice surgery) instruction set available to surface codes. Some work, however, has suggested that direct compilation from Clifford+T to lattice surgery operations may be beneficial for circuits that have high degrees of logical parallelism. In this study, we analyze the resource costs for implementing Hamiltonian simulation using example approaches from each of these leading surface code compilation families. The Hamiltonians whose dynamics we consider are those of the transverse-field Ising model in several geometries, the Kitaev honeycomb model, and the [MATH] complex under a time-varying magnetic field. We show, among other things, that the optimal scheme depends on whether Hamiltonian simulation is implemented using the quantum signal processing or Trotter-Suzuki algorithms, with Trotterization benefiting by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation for these applications. Our results suggest that surface code quantum computers should not have a one-size-fits-all compilation scheme, but that smart compilers should predict the optimal scheme based upon high-level quantities from logical circuits such as average circuit density, numbers of logical qubits, and T fraction.

.
tldr: This paper compares two surface code compilation schemes for Hamiltonian simulation, showing that the optimal approach depends on the algorithm used.
motivation: To determine whether serializing Clifford gates or direct Clifford+T compilation is more resource-efficient for fault-tolerant quantum computing, as prior work suggested the latter may benefit parallel circuits.
method: The authors analyze resource costs for Hamiltonian simulation of several models (transverse-field Ising, Kitaev honeycomb, etc.) using quantum signal processing and Trotter-Suzuki algorithms, comparing two compilation families.
result: Trotterization benefits by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation, while QSP may favor serialization; the optimal scheme depends on circuit density, qubit count, and T fraction.
conclusion: Surface code quantum computers should use adaptive compilation strategies rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

title: Disorder-Induced Entanglement Phase Transitions In Non-Hermitian Systems With Skin Effects
authors: Kai Li, Ze-Chuan Liu, And Yong Xu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2186 (2026).

Non-Hermitian dynamics is ubiquitous in various physical systems. While recent study shows that such a dynamics leads to an area-law scaling of the entanglement entropy due to the non-Hermitian skin effects, it remains unclear how disorder changes the behavior of the entanglement entropy in a non-Hermitian system with skin effects. Here we study the dynamics of a many-body state of free fermions in the paradigmatic Hatano-Nelson model with open boundaries, and find that the area-law behavior of the entanglement entropy in the pristine Hatano-Nelson model develops into a logarithmic scaling for small disorder strength. As we further increase the disorder strength, the system reenters an area-law regime through an entanglement phase transition. At the critical point, the entanglement entropy exhibits a universal algebraic scaling. We further demonstrate the absence of a conformal invariance in the log-law regime by examining the subsystem entanglement entropy, the connected correlation function and the mutual information. Finally, we show the existence of disorder induced entanglement phase transitions in the Hatano-Nelson model with periodic boundaries.

.
tldr: This paper studies disorder-induced entanglement phase transitions in non-Hermitian systems with skin effects, showing transitions between area-law and logarithmic scaling of entanglement entropy.
motivation: Understanding how disorder affects entanglement dynamics in non-Hermitian systems with skin effects is an open question, relevant to quantum thermodynamics and information processing in open systems.
method: The authors analyze the dynamics of free fermions in the Hatano-Nelson model with open and periodic boundaries, computing entanglement entropy, connected correlation functions, and mutual information for varying disorder strengths.
result: They find that small disorder changes area-law to logarithmic scaling, and stronger disorder restores area-law via an entanglement phase transition, with algebraic scaling at criticality and absence of conformal invariance in the log-law regime.
conclusion: The work reveals disorder-induced entanglement phase transitions in non-Hermitian systems, providing insights into the interplay of disorder, non-Hermiticity, and entanglement, with implications for quantum information processing in open systems.

title: Promise Of Graph Sparsification And Decomposition For Noise Reduction In Qaoa: Analysis For Trapped-Ion Compilations
authors: Jai Moondra, Phillip C. Lotshaw, Greg Mohler, And Swati Gupta
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2185 (2026).

We develop new approximate compilation schemes that significantly reduce the expense of compiling the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for solving the Max-Cut problem. Our main focus is on compilation with trapped-ion simulators using Pauli-[MATH] operations and all-to-all Ising Hamiltonian [MATH] evolution generated by Molmer-Sorensen or optical dipole force interactions, though some of our results also apply to standard gate-based compilations. Our results are based on principles of graph sparsification and decomposition; the former reduces the number of edges in a graph while maintaining its cut structure, while the latter breaks a weighted graph into a small number of unweighted graphs. Though these techniques have been used as heuristics in various hybrid quantum algorithms, there have been no guarantees on their performance, to the best of our knowledge. This work provides the first provable guarantees using sparsification and decomposition to improve quantum noise resilience and reduce quantum circuit complexity. For quantum hardware that uses edge-by-edge QAOA compilations, sparsification leads to a direct reduction in circuit complexity. For trapped-ion quantum simulators implementing all-to-all [MATH] pulses, we show that for a [MATH] factor loss in the Max-Cut approximation ([MATH], our compilations improve the (worst-case) number of [MATH] pulses from [MATH] to [MATH] and the (worst-case) number of Pauli-[MATH] bit flips from [MATH] to [MATH] for [MATH]-node graphs. This is an asymptotic improvement for any constant [MATH]. We demonstrate that significant improvements to the approximation ratio are obtained using decomposition in simulated trapped-ion experiments with dephasing noise. We further present a generic argument showing that sparsification results in an exponentially improved circuit fidelity lower bound in digital computing schemes based on one- and two-qubit gates, which are relevant to a wide variety of hardwares such as superconducting qubits and certain neutral atom or trapped ion setups, and more sophisticated noise models. We anticipate these approximate compilation techniques will be useful tools in a variety of future quantum computing experiments.

.
tldr: This paper provides the first provable guarantees for using graph sparsification and decomposition to reduce circuit complexity and improve noise resilience in QAOA for Max-Cut, with applications to trapped-ion and gate-based quantum computing.
motivation: QAOA compilation for Max-Cut is resource-intensive and noise-sensitive; graph sparsification and decomposition have been used heuristically but lack theoretical guarantees.
method: The authors develop approximate compilation schemes based on graph sparsification (reducing edges while preserving cut structure) and decomposition (breaking weighted graphs into unweighted ones), and analyze their impact on circuit complexity and noise resilience for trapped-ion and gate-based implementations.
result: They prove asymptotic improvements in the number of Molmer-Sorensen pulses and Pauli-X bit flips for trapped-ion simulators, and show exponentially improved circuit fidelity lower bounds for digital schemes, with simulations demonstrating improved approximation ratios under dephasing noise.
conclusion: These techniques offer practical tools for reducing quantum circuit complexity and enhancing noise resilience in QAOA, with broad applicability to various quantum hardware.

title: Entanglement Growth In The Dark Intervals Of A Locally Monitored Free-fermion Chain
authors: Giovanni Di Fresco, Youenn Le Gal, Davide Valenti, Marco Schiró, And Angelo Carollo
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2183 (2026).

We consider a free fermionic chain with monitoring of the particle density on a single site of the chain and study the entanglement dynamics of quantum jump trajectories. We show that the entanglement entropy grows in time towards a stationary state which display volume law scaling of the entropy, in stark contrast with both the unitary dynamics after a local quench and the no-click limit corresponding to full post-selection. We explain the extensive entanglement growth as a consequence of the peculiar distribution of quantum jumps in time, which display superpoissonian waiting time distribution characterised by a bunching of quantum jumps followed by long dark intervals where no-clicks are detected, akin to the distribution of fluorescence light in a driven atom. We show that the presence of dark intervals is the key feature to explain the effect and that by increasing the number of sites which are monitored the volume law scaling gives away to the Zeno effect and its associated area law.

.
tldr: This paper studies entanglement growth in a free-fermion chain under local monitoring, showing that quantum jumps with super-Poissonian statistics and dark intervals lead to volume-law entanglement, contrasting with unitary and no-click limits.
motivation: Understanding how measurement-induced dynamics affect entanglement in many-body systems is crucial for quantum information processing and thermalization.
method: The authors analyze a free-fermion chain with local density monitoring, using quantum jump trajectories and waiting time distributions to characterize entanglement dynamics.
result: They find that entanglement entropy grows to a stationary volume-law state due to bunching of quantum jumps and long dark intervals, while increasing monitored sites leads to Zeno effect and area law.
conclusion: The work highlights the role of measurement statistics in driving entanglement growth, offering insights into monitored quantum systems and their thermodynamic behavior.

title: On The Quantum Computational Complexity Of Classical Linear Dynamics With Geometrically Local Interactions: Dequantization And Universality
authors: Kazuki Sakamoto And Keisuke Fujii
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2182 (2026).

The simulation of large-scale classical systems in exponentially small space on quantum computers has gained attention. The prior work demonstrated that a quantum algorithm offers an exponential speedup over any classical algorithm in simulating classical dynamics with long-range interactions. However, many real-world classical systems, such as those arising from partial differential equations, exhibit only local interactions. The question remains whether quantum algorithms can still provide exponential speedup under this condition. In this work, we thoroughly characterize the computational complexity of simulating such geometrically local systems on quantum computers. First, we dequantize the quantum algorithm for simulating short-time (polynomial-time) dynamics of such systems. This implies that the problem of simulating this dynamics does not yield any exponential quantum advantage. Second, we show that simulating short-time dynamics is at least as hard as polynomial-time and linear-space probabilistic classical computation. Third, we show that the computational complexity of simulating long-time (exponential-time) dynamics is captured by exponential-time and polynomial-space quantum computation. This suggests a super-polynomial time advantage when restricting the computation to polynomial-space, or an exponential space advantage otherwise. This work offers new insights into the complexity of classical dynamics governed by partial differential equations, providing a pathway for achieving quantum advantage in practical problems.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the quantum computational complexity of simulating classical linear dynamics with geometrically local interactions, showing no exponential quantum advantage for short-time dynamics but potential super-polynomial advantage for long-time dynamics under space constraints.
motivation: The authors aim to determine whether quantum computers can provide exponential speedups for simulating classical systems with local interactions, which are common in real-world PDEs, as opposed to the previously studied long-range interactions.
method: They dequantize the quantum algorithm for short-time dynamics, prove a lower bound relating it to probabilistic classical computation, and analyze the complexity of long-time dynamics in terms of quantum complexity classes.
result: Short-time dynamics simulation has no exponential quantum advantage and is as hard as polynomial-time linear-space probabilistic computation; long-time dynamics is captured by exponential-time polynomial-space quantum computation, suggesting super-polynomial time advantage under space restrictions.
conclusion: The work provides a thorough complexity characterization, offering insights into when quantum advantage may be achievable for simulating classical dynamics with local interactions.

title: Atommovr: An Open-source Simulation Framework For Rearrangement In Atomic Arrays
authors: Nikhil K Harle, Bo-Yu Chen, Bob Bao, And Hannes Bernien
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2177 (2026).

The task of atom rearrangement has emerged in the last decade as a fundamental building block in the development of neutral atom-based quantum processors. As such processors grow to thousands of atoms, it becomes increasingly important to design algorithms robust to experimental sources of error. While recent progress has been made towards developing algorithms with favorable time scaling, such work has been limited to noiseless settings. Moreover, there is a lack of open-source code for reproducing and benchmarking existing algorithms. To address these deficiencies, we develop an open-source simulation framework, atommovr, and leverage it to study three distinct settings: 1) time-optimal, noiseless rearrangement, 2) noisy rearrangement under realistic error models, and 3) noiseless dual-species rearrangement. We extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, study advantageous strategies across different error regimes, and develop a novel dual-species algorithm, InsideOut, capable of avoiding 'blocked' configurations with a near-unity success rate. We hope that atommovr can serve as a common tool for the community to study rearrangement, lower the barrier to entry for new experimental groups, and stimulate progress in developing algorithms tailored to minimize atom loss in experiment.

.
tldr: This paper introduces an open-source simulation framework for atom rearrangement in neutral atom arrays, benchmarking algorithms under noisy and dual-species conditions.
motivation: As neutral atom quantum processors scale to thousands of atoms, efficient and robust rearrangement algorithms are crucial, yet existing work lacks open-source tools and noise robustness.
method: The authors develop 'atommovr', a simulation framework, and use it to study time-optimal noiseless rearrangement, noisy rearrangement with realistic error models, and noiseless dual-species rearrangement, including a novel dual-species algorithm 'InsideOut'.
result: They extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, identify advantageous strategies across error regimes, and demonstrate that InsideOut avoids blocked configurations with near-unity success rate.
conclusion: The framework provides a common benchmarking tool for the community, lowering entry barriers and stimulating progress in atom-loss-minimizing algorithms.

title: Pilot-Wave Simulator: Exact Classical Sampling From Ideal And Noisy Quantum Circuits Up To Hundreds Of Qubits
authors: Gleb Kalachev, Pavel Mosharev, Zuoheng Zou, Pavel Panteleev, And Man-Hong Yung
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2173 (2026).

Quantum circuit simulators running on classical computers offer a vital platform for designing, testing, and optimizing quantum algorithms, driving innovation despite limited access to real quantum hardware. However, their scalability is inherently constrained by exponential memory and computational overhead, which restricts accurate simulation of large-scale quantum circuits and often results in approximate output distributions. Here, we propose an exact sampling algorithm that integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, wherein a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. As a demonstration, we target the challenge of generating samples from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating both depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models. These results enable further validation of several assumptions and conjectures at a scale previously out of reach, significantly expanding the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research.

.
tldr: This paper presents an exact classical sampling algorithm for quantum circuits up to hundreds of qubits by combining tensor network contraction with a Markov process, demonstrated on QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits under noise.
motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is crucial for benchmarking and developing quantum algorithms, but scalability is limited by exponential overhead. The authors aim to extend the reach of exact sampling to larger circuits, enabling validation of quantum advantage conjectures.
method: The algorithm integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, where a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit, allowing exact sampling from the output distribution.
result: They demonstrate exact sampling from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models, achieving a scale previously out of reach.
conclusion: This work significantly expands the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research, providing a tool to test assumptions and conjectures at larger scales, which is relevant to quantum information and complexity studies.

title: Hoare Meets Heisenberg: A Lightweight Logic For Quantum Programs
authors: Aarthi Sundaram, Robert Rand, Kartik Singhal, Youngchan Cho, And Brad Lackey
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2172 (2026).

We show that Gottesman's (1998) semantics for Clifford circuits based on the Heisenberg representation gives rise to a lightweight Hoare-like logic for efficiently characterizing a common subset of quantum programs. Our applications include (i) certifying whether auxiliary qubits can be safely disposed of, (ii) determining if a system is separable across a given bipartition, (iii) checking the transversality of a gate with respect to a given stabilizer code, and (iv) computing post-measurement states for computational basis measurements. Further, this logic is extended to accommodate universal quantum computing by deriving Hoare triples for the [MATH]-gate, multiply-controlled unitaries such as the Toffoli gate, and some gate injection circuits that use associated magic states. A number of interesting results emerge from this logic, including a lower bound on the number of [MATH] gates necessary to perform a multiply-controlled [MATH] gate.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a lightweight Hoare-like logic for quantum programs based on Gottesman's Heisenberg representation, enabling efficient certification of properties like qubit disposal, separability, and gate transversality.
motivation: To provide a practical, lightweight verification method for quantum programs, particularly those involving Clifford circuits and stabilizer codes, which are common in quantum error correction and fault tolerance.
method: The authors formalize a Hoare logic using Gottesman's semantics for Clifford circuits, deriving Hoare triples for Clifford operations and extending to universal quantum computing via the T-gate, Toffoli, and magic state injection.
result: The logic enables certification of auxiliary qubit disposal, separability across bipartitions, transversality of gates with respect to stabilizer codes, and computation of post-measurement states. It also yields a lower bound on the number of T-gates needed for multiply-controlled gates.
conclusion: The proposed logic offers a lightweight and efficient approach to reasoning about quantum programs, with applications in quantum error correction and resource management, though it is limited to a subset of quantum programs.

title: Cascaded Optomechanical Sensing For Small Signals
authors: Marta Maria Marchese, Daniel Braun, Stefan Nimmrichter And Dennis Rätzel
abstract: We propose a sensing scheme for detecting weak forces that achieves sensitivity scaling proportional to the number of individual sensors without relying on entanglement or other non-classical resources. Our scheme utilizes coherent averaging across a chain of optomechanical cavities, unidirectionally coupled via a laser beam. As the beam passes through the cavities, it accumulates phase shifts induced by a common external force acting on the mechanical elements. Remarkably, this fully classical approach achieves the sensitivity scaling typically associated with quantum-enhanced protocols, providing a robust and experimentally feasible route to precision sensing. Potential applications range from high-sensitivity gravitational field measurements at the Large Hadron Collider to probing dark matter interactions and detecting gravitational waves. This work opens a new pathway for leveraging coherent light-matter interactions for force sensing.
tldr: This paper proposes a cascaded optomechanical sensing scheme that achieves sensitivity scaling with the number of sensors using only classical resources, offering a robust alternative to quantum-enhanced protocols.
motivation: The authors aim to achieve quantum-enhanced sensitivity scaling without relying on fragile non-classical resources, making high-precision force sensing more experimentally feasible.
method: They model a chain of optomechanical cavities unidirectionally coupled by a laser beam, where a common external force induces phase shifts that accumulate coherently as the beam passes through each cavity.
result: The scheme achieves sensitivity scaling proportional to the number of sensors, matching the scaling of quantum-enhanced protocols, and is robust against imperfections.
conclusion: This work provides a practical pathway for precision sensing applications such as gravitational wave detection and dark matter searches, leveraging coherent light-matter interactions.

title: Quantum To Classical Relaxation Dynamics Of The Dissipative Rydberg Gas
authors: Viktoria Noel And Igor Lesanovsky
abstract: We investigate the relaxation dynamics of a Rydberg gas in regimes where coherent processes and dissipation compete. In the strongly dissipative limit, the dynamics is known to be governed by an effective classical rate equation and to exhibit kinetically constrained, glassy relaxation towards a trivial stationary state. This behaviour originates from the Rydberg blockade, which prevents simultaneous excitations within a characteristic blockade radius.
